outline.chapter_title: The Alleged Pump-and-Dump Scheme and the District Court’s Dismissal
outline.description: This chapter introduces the factual allegations, the defendants’ social-media-based trading activity, the charged offenses, and the procedural path that brought the case to the Fifth Circuit. It explains why the district court dismissed the indictment and frames the core dispute on appeal.
subtopics: Who the defendants were and why their large social-media followings mattered
How the alleged pump-and-dump scheme worked: buying first, promoting with false or misleading posts, inflating price, then secretly selling
The government’s allegation that the scheme generated $114 million in profits
The charges: conspiracy to commit securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1349 and substantive securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 and 2
Knight’s guilty plea and the remaining defendants’ motion to dismiss
The district court’s reasoning: the indictment allegedly described only deprivation of valuable economic information, not a traditional property interest
The government’s appeal and the Fifth Circuit’s task in reviewing the dismissal

outline.chapter_title: How to Evaluate an Indictment: Review Standard and the Securities Fraud Framework
outline.description: This chapter sets out the legal framework the Fifth Circuit used before reaching the merits. It explains how courts test the sufficiency of an indictment, what must be alleged, and how § 1348 is interpreted through concepts borrowed from mail and wire fraud law.
subtopics: De novo review of a district court’s dismissal of an indictment
The rule that a court must take the indictment’s factual allegations as true at the dismissal stage
The three core functions of an indictment: pleading the elements, providing notice, and protecting against double jeopardy
The requirement that the indictment allege each material element of the offense
The text of 18 U.S.C. § 1348 and its two fraud formulations
Why Fifth Circuit courts look to mail and wire fraud precedents to interpret securities fraud under § 1348
The two operative elements identified by the Fifth Circuit: a scheme to defraud and an intent to defraud
The opinion’s baseline definitions: material misrepresentation, deception to obtain something of value, and intent to deceive plus cause harm through deceit

outline.chapter_title: Scheme to Defraud: Traditional Property, Fraudulent Inducement, and the Limits of Ciminelli
outline.description: This chapter addresses the defendants’ first merits argument: that the indictment failed to allege deprivation of money or property. It explains the Supreme Court’s rejection of the right-to-control theory in Ciminelli and why the Fifth Circuit held that this indictment instead alleged a valid fraudulent-inducement theory aimed at obtaining victims’ money.
subtopics: The defendants’ property-based objection to the indictment
Ciminelli’s rejection of the right-to-control theory as a basis for federal fraud liability
What the right-to-control theory means: depriving a victim of potentially valuable economic information used to make discretionary economic decisions
Why valuable economic information alone is not a traditional property interest under the federal fraud statutes
How the Fifth Circuit distinguished this case from Ciminelli
The indictment’s actual theory: defendants used misrepresentations to induce followers to purchase securities
Why inducing investors to buy securities means inducing them to part with money or property
The role of Kousisis in identifying fraudulent inducement as a legitimate fraud theory
The court’s conclusion that the indictment alleged more than informational deprivation and therefore stated a cognizable scheme to defraud

outline.chapter_title: Intent to Defraud: Why Profit-Seeking Can Satisfy the Statute Even Without Net Economic Loss
outline.description: This chapter examines the defendants’ second merits argument: that they intended only to profit, not to harm anyone. It shows how the Fifth Circuit relied on Kousisis to reject any requirement that the government plead a scheme to leave victims economically worse off, and why fraudulent inducement to spend money is enough.
subtopics: The defendants’ argument that intent to profit is different from intent to harm
Kousisis and the modern fraudulent-inducement theory
The Supreme Court’s holding that fraud statutes do not require proof that the defendant sought to inflict net pecuniary loss
Why obtaining the victim’s money or property through deception is enough, even if the victim receives something of equivalent market value
The indictment’s allegations showing intent: false and misleading posts designed to induce other investors to purchase securities
Why receiving market-value securities did not defeat the fraud theory at the pleading stage
The Fifth Circuit’s point that the defendants ‘had money in mind’ because the object of the scheme was to profit from induced purchases
The court’s treatment of injury: fraud is complete upon inducing the transfer of money or property under materially false pretenses
The significance of the Fifth Circuit’s reference to Baker and the Seventh Circuit’s Smith decision in rejecting a strict victim-loss/defendant-gain symmetry requirement

outline.chapter_title: Holding, Remand, and the Case’s Place in Post-Ciminelli Securities Fraud Law
outline.description: This chapter synthesizes the Fifth Circuit’s holding, explains the immediate procedural consequence, and highlights the opinion’s practical and doctrinal significance for securities-fraud indictments based on social-media promotion and market manipulation.
subtopics: The holding: the indictment sufficiently alleged both a scheme to defraud and an intent to defraud
The disposition: reversal of the district court’s dismissal and remand for further proceedings
What the Fifth Circuit did not decide: guilt, evidentiary sufficiency at trial, or the truth of the allegations
How the case clarifies that Ciminelli does not bar fraud charges whenever misinformation affects economic decisions
How Kousisis broadens the understanding of injury in fraudulent-inducement cases involving securities transactions
Why the opinion matters for prosecutions of pump-and-dump schemes carried out through social media
The case’s broader lesson for pleading federal fraud: allegations must connect deception to obtaining money or property, not merely to withholding useful information
